analysis.one_liner: Mandates oil and gas lease sales, fast-tracks pipeline and export permits, and curbs federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to hold a minimum number of oil and gas lease sales every year on federal land and in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska. It would set hard deadlines for approving pipelines and natural gas exports, automatically approve applications that miss a 60-day clock, and retroactively approve all natural gas export applications filed between 2020 and 2025. It would also stop the President from limiting drilling or mining on federal land without a new act of Congress, and reinstate several lighter-touch Trump-era environmental and oil-and-gas rules — and lock them in place for 15 years.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, pipeline companies, coal companies, and natural gas exporters gain guaranteed access to federal land and water, faster permits, and weaker environmental review. Renewable and geothermal developers gain designated leasing areas and a faster path for exploration test projects.

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least four oil and gas lease sales a year in each of ten states, plus two annual sales each in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska offshore regions, offering all eligible parcels.

Gives federal agencies one year to approve natural gas pipeline and transmission projects, and orders FERC to issue pipeline certificates without further proceedings for projects that meet safety rules.
Requires natural gas export decisions within 60 days and deems all export applications submitted between 2020 and 2025 approved.

Makes drilling permit applications 'deemed approved' if the Interior Department has not decided within 60 days, and bars the President from restricting drilling, mining, or leasing on federal land without a new act of Congress.
Reinstates the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule, the 2020 methane rule, the 2020 NEPA regulations, and other deregulatory rules, and prohibits any modification of them for 15 years.
Limits environmental review under NEPA to effects 'in the United States,' narrowing what federal agencies must consider for projects with impacts abroad or in U.S. waters.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and communities near leased public land, pipelines, and export facilities bear increased pollution risk and loss of public input, since environmental review is shortened or bypassed. Consumers could face higher domestic natural gas prices as more gas is committed to exports.

drawbacks.text: A 60-day deemed-approval clock and one-year permit deadlines would pressure agencies to approve projects before completing environmental and endangered-species reviews.
Retroactively approving every export application filed from 2020 to 2025 would skip review entirely for those projects.
Freezing the reinstated water, methane, NEPA, and valuation rules for 15 years would prevent agencies from updating them even if new health or environmental evidence emerges.
Narrowing NEPA to domestic effects would exclude from review harm that U.S.-funded projects cause abroad or in waters beyond the exclusive economic zone.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that permitting review can be slow, but this bill replaces that concern with mandatory approvals and rule-freezes rather than targeted reform, and its drafters offered no estimate of the added pollution or fiscal cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow mostly to energy producers through guaranteed access to public land and faster, weaker review; the costs — more emissions, less public input, and locked-in deregulatory rules — fall on communities and taxpayers. The small provisions for geothermal and renewable leasing do not change the bill's overall tilt, and the 15-year rule freeze plus retroactive export approvals make it unusually rigid even as deregulatory bills go.

outcome.mechanism: Sen. Cruz introduced it alone and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never took it up, so it died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill in the Senate on March 21, 2023, with no cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day it was introduced; that is the last action recorded.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing environmental review requirements, the President's authority over federal land and cross-border energy projects, and the ability of agencies to update energy rules all remain intact — communities near federal lease land, pipelines, and export terminals are better off than they would have been had it passed, while oil, gas, and coal producers lost the access and faster permits it would have guaranteed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near federal lease land and pipelines

sides.party_line_note: No senator from either party cosponsored the bill — zero of 49 Republicans and zero of 48 Democrats — and it never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: Mandated lease sales on federal land and offshore, 60-day deemed-approved drilling permits, and a ban on new moratoria without Congress would lock in cheap access to public land. The cost is borne by communities near drilling and by air and water quality.

The bill sets a 60-day export approval deadline and retroactively approves every export application filed from 2020 to 2025. Shipping more gas abroad supports export profits but tends to raise domestic gas prices for U.S. consumers.

One-year approval deadlines, automatic certificates for projects meeting safety rules, and elimination of the presidential permit for cross-border pipelines remove the main points where communities and the public could weigh in. Landowners and towns along routes lose leverage.
The bill bars new moratoria on coal leasing without an act of Congress, protecting the industry's access to federal coal. Continued federal coal mining increases emissions and local pollution.

The bill requires designated priority leasing areas for geothermal, solar, and wind and creates a categorical exclusion from environmental review for geothermal exploration test projects. This is the bill's main genuine benefit to lower-carbon energy, though it is a small share of the bill.

industries.industry: Environmental review and oversight (agencies and affected communities)
industries.note: NEPA would be narrowed to domestic effects, four deregulatory rules would be reinstated and frozen for 15 years, and agencies would face approval deadlines that effectively force permits. The public loses its main channel for input on federal energy projects.
